newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: New Congo says mines must bring social benefits.
newsitem.headline: New Congo says mines must bring social benefits.

text.p: Mining companies wanting to deal with Laurent Kabila's government in the Democratic Republic of Congo must be prepared to work for social development as well as profits, the mines minister said on Tuesday.

Mututulo Kambale said it was one way in which the former Zaire could translate its vast mineral resources to quickly benefit the impoverished country and bring benefits to its more than 40 million people.
"Social involvement is of great importance, it's a prerequisite I should say for signing agreements," Mututulo told Reuters in an interview.

Kabila's government is faced with the challenge of rebuilding Africa's third largest country after over three decades of decline through corruption and lack of investment under President Mobutu Sese Seko who was ousted two weeks ago.
Foreign mining companies, scared off for years by Congo's instability, have rushed to try to secure a slice of the action in one of the world's last mining regions to be left barely touched.

Executives from some of the world's biggest mining houses have headed for Kinshasa with proposals in their briefcases for exploiting reserves of copper, cobalt, zinc and tin as well as gold, diamonds and other minerals.
Mututulo said there was no specific requirement in terms of percentage of profits or investment which companies had to spend on development projects.
"We insist on social involvement because imagine if people came and they found people barefoot and when they finish exploiting the region they are still barefoot," said Mututulo.
"If they can build some roads, some schools, some hospitals then that is fine."

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) has said it is committed to free market principles. But among the government are many one-time Marxists, including Kabila himself.
Mututulo said the government favoured joint ventures with mining companies in which foreign investors had a majority stake.
He said the privatisation of central Kasai-based state diamond mines MIBA and southern Katanga-based copper, cobalt and zinc mines GECAMINES was not under consideration.
Even before the AFDL took power, American Mineral Fields had signed a deal for rights to a copper and cobalt tailings project in Katanga, and said it would built a 200,000 tonnes a year zinc plant.

Mututulo said the Lundin group, behind the Tenke Mining Corporation, had already paid the government $50 million, after its copper and cobalt deal signed with a previous government was ratified by the AFDL.

On Tuesday Mututulo said he had signed a preliminary agreement with Russell Resources Group for gold exploration in the northeastern corner of Congo. He did not say what scale of investment the group foresees.
Agreements already signed during the Mobutu era are being reviewed and in some cases are up for renegotiation.

Mututulo said a concession of over 80,000 sq km, leased by Barrick Gold Corporation in northeastern Congo, was one of several old contracts under review. He would not say what changes to the lease the government was asking for.

"We try to ratify agreements made by the former government because we accept the principle of continuity...if there is something we don't accept we will ask the people to change in the benefit of both parties," Mututulo said.
"It is not good to have very huge concessions in the hands of one company, it is better for more companies to have a chance," he added.

Kabila's government has already reorganised the mechanism for buying diamonds from the MIBA mine in Mbuji-Mayi, most of which formerly went to De Beers. It now insists that companies compete at auction for the largely industrial stones.
Taking part in the next auction on June 10 are De Beers, Susskind, American Diamond Buyers and Carat SPRL.
In the mid-1980s Zaire produced some 500,000 tonnes of copper a year but last year output was only 40,000 tonnes. Cobalt output has dropped from 15,000 to around 4,000 tonnes.
